AWAR D 1.

Vide this award, I shall decide the present claim petition under section 166 & 140 of Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, filed by the petitioner Preeti Rana seeking compensation on _____________________________________________________________ account of grievous injury caused due to a motor vehicular accident occurred on 05.01.2016 at 08:30 a.m. at Village Hisavda More, Baghpat Road, Baghpat, U.P., involving an Indico Car, bearing registration no. PB10-FM-5117 (in short "offending vehicle"), being driven by respondent no.1.
In connection with this accident, FIR no. 02/2016, u/s 279/338/427 IPC was registered at PS Singhavali Ahir.

2. The brief facts of the case as emerged from the petition are that on the aforesaid date and time,
petitioner along with Laxmi Jain was going from Gautam Budh Nagar to Ameenagar Sarai, Baghpat Preeti Rana (Injured) vs Rakesh (Driver) on 20 April, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/37672764/
1 in a car bearing no. UP14BR-1325 and when they reached at the aforesaid place, the aforesaid offending vehicle, being driven by respondent no.1 Rakesh in rash and negligent manner, came from Baghpat side and hit their vehicle.
As a result of the accident, petitioner sustained grievous injuries.
She was immediately taken to a local hospital and then was shifted to St. Stephens Hospital, Delhi.

It has been alleged that accident took place due to rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle, which was being driven by respondent no.1, owned by respondent no.2 and insured with respondent no.3.
With these submissions, the petitioner has claimed compensation of Rs.50 lakhs along with interest.
3. In response to notice of the petition, only respondent no.3/ insurance company filed written statement.
Respondent no.1 & 2 were proceeded ex-parte vide order dated 04.07.2017 and 21.09.2017 respectively.
_____________________________ 3.1 Respondent no.3/ insurance company in its written statement denied the responsibility to pay compensation by taking general defences.

The offending vehicle was admittedly insured with the insurance company but it has been contended that liability of insurer is subject to the compliance of terms and conditions of the insurance policy.

4. Upon completion of pleadings, following issues were framed by my Ld. Predecessor on on 18.01.2018, as under:
i).

Whether respondent no.1 was driving vehicle, bearing no. PB-10FM-5117 05.01.2016 at 08:30 a.m. at Village Hisavda More, at a high speed and in rash and negligent manner and hit against the vehicle bearing no. UP14BR-1325, as a result its occupant namely petitioner sustained injuries?

Whether respondent no.1 was driving vehicle, bearing no. PB-10FM-5117 05.01.2016 at 08:30 a.m. at Village Hisavda More, at a high speed and in rash and negligent manner and hit against the vehicle bearing no. UP14BR-1325, as a result its occupant namely petitioner sustained injuries?
OPP 9.
It is settled law
that an action founded on the principle of fault liability, the proof of rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle is sine qua non.

However, the standard of proof is not as s t r i c t a s a p p l i e d i n c r i m i n a l c a s e s a n d e v i d e n c e i s t o b e _____________________________________________________________ tested on the touchstone of preponderance of probabilities.
Holistic view is to be taken while dealing with the Claim Petition based upon negligence.
Strict rules of evidence are not applicable in an inquiry conducted by the Claims Tribunal.

Reference may be made to the judgments titled as New India Assurance Co. Ltd. v. Sakshi Bhutani & Others., MAC APP. No. 550/2011 decided on 02.07.2012,
Bimla Devi & Others v. Himachal Road Transport Corporation & Others (2009) 13 SC 530,
Parmeshwari v. Amirchand & Others 2011 (1) SCR 1096 & Mangla Ram v. Oriental Insurance Company Ltd. & Others 2018, Law Suit (SC) 303.

sentences.text: In order to prove her case, the petitioner as PW1 testified that on 05.01.2016 at 08:30 a.m. she alongwith Laxmi Jain was going in a car, bearing no. UP14-BR-1325, belonging to complainant Deepak Tyagi, driven by his driver PW2 Sachin and when they reached at Village Hisavda More, an Indigo car, bearing registration no. PB10-FM- 5117, driven by respondent no.1, came from Baghpat side at a very high speed, rashly and negligently and hit the car of petitioner. PW1/ petitioner further deposed that as a result of the accident, she alongwith other occupants of car received grievous injuries.

11. During her cross-examination by learned counsel for insurance company, PW1 (petitioner/
injured) clarified the manner of accident and mentioned that the offending vehicle came from the front side and hit their vehicle and the accident had taken place on the left hand side of the road.
She added that her vehicle was being driven on its correct lane.
Further, she _____________________________________________________________ denied the suggestion that the accident had occurred due to the negligent driving of her driver Sachin.
12. PW2 Sachin, another eye-witness deposed on the same lines and supported the version of PW1 (petitioner).
He testified that he was the driver at vehicle, bearing no. UP14BR-1325.

He further deposed that when said vehicle boarded by injured reached at turn, near Pilana Bhatta, Baghpat,
suddenly an Indigo car came from front side at a high speed of about 90 kmph and hit against his vehicle from front side.
PW2 made it clear that he was driving his vehicle in his lane in left side and was on the moderate speed of about 30-35 kmph.
He deposed that he along with injured received injuries in the accident and that police seized the offending vehicle and arrested the driver.
During cross-examination, this witness denied the suggestion that driver of the offending vehicle was not at fault.
He also denied the suggestion that accident had taken place due to his negligence.

13. A conjoint reading of the testimony of both the eye- witnesses (PW1 & PW2) and documents placed on record including the certified copy of FIR (Ex.PW1/1), certified copy of charge-sheet Preeti Rana (Injured) vs Rakesh (Driver) on 20 April, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/37672764/
4 (Ex.PW1/2) and certified copy of site plan of the place of accident (Ex.PW1/4) clearly support their version with respect to the rash and negligent driving of offending vehicle by respondent no.1.

Also,
in the cross-examination of eye-witnesses (PW1 and PW2), I found no such contradiction or inconsistency which could create any doubt upon the veracity of their testimonies.

Thus, the evidence of eye-witnesses in this case on the aspect of rash and negligent act of respondent no.1 while _____________________________________________________________ driving the offending vehicle remained unimpeached and hence, the same is to be accepted on its face value itself.

14. Further, the respondent no.1, the driver of the offending vehicle was the best witness, who could have stepped into the witness box to challenge the testimony of the petitioner (PW1) regarding the above accident and its manner but he preferred not to enter into the witness box during the course of inquiry.

Thus, an adverse inference is liable to be drawn against him to the effect that the accident in question occurred due to rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle by him in view of the law laid down in case of Cholamandalam M.S. General Insurance Company Ltd. v. Kamlesh,
2009(3) AD (Delhi) 310.
15.

Besides, discharge summaries of the petitioner clearly shows the alleged history of RTA and that the petitioner suffered fracture of shaft of femur with neck of femur left side, fracture of shaft of femur right side, fractures of tibial spine, shaft of tibia right and fracture of patella left.
18.

In view of above, it is held that respondent no.1 was rash and negligent in driving the offending vehicle and he hit the petitioner's vehicle, as a result of which, petitioner sustained grievous injuries.
Accordingly, issue no.1 is answered in favour of petitioner and against the respondents.

ISSUE NO.2 :
Whether the petitioner is entitled for any compensation, if so, to what amount and from whom?
OPP 19.

In view of the finding on Issue no.1, petitioner is entitled to get compensation, however,
quantum of compensation still needs to be adjudicated.

Section 168 of Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 enjoins upon the claim Tribunal to hold an inquiry into the claim to make an award determining the amount of compensation, which appears to be just and reasonable.
As per settled law, compensation is not expected to be windfall or a bonanza nor it should be pittance

A man is not compensated for the physical injury, he is compensated for the loss which he suffers as a result of that injury (Baker v.
Willoughby (1970) Ac 467 at page 492 per Lord Reid).

2 0 . T h e p r e s e n t c l a i m p e t i t i o n p e r t a i n s t o i n j u r y a n d s c o p e _____________________________________________________________ of compensation in injury cases has been considered by Hon'ble Supreme Court in case titled as Mr.
R.D. Hattangadi v. M/S Pest Control (India) Pvt. Ltd., 1995 AIR 755.

entities.text: R.D. Hattangadi v. M/S Pest Control (India) Pvt. Ltd., 1995 AIR 755
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
The relevant extract is as under:
"Broadly speaking while fixing an amount of compensation payable to a victim of an accident, the damages have to be assessed separately as pecuniary damages and special damages.

Pecuniary damages are those which the victim has actually incurred and which is capable of being calculated in terms of money-, whereas non-pecuniary damages are those which are incapable of being assessed by arithmetical calculations.

In order to appreciate two concepts pecuniary damages may, include expenses Preeti Rana (Injured) vs Rakesh (Driver) on 20 April, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/37672764/
6 incurred by the claimant: (i) medical attendance; (ii) loss of earning of profit upto the date of trial; (iii) other material loss.

So far non- pecuniary damages are concerned,
they may include (i) damages for mental and physical shock, pain suffering, already suffered or likely to be suffered in future; (ii) damages to compensate for the loss of amenities of life which may include a variety of matters i.e. on account of injury the claimant may not be able to walk, run or sit; (iii) damages for the loss of expectation of life, i.e. on account of injury the normal longevity of the person concerned is shortened; (iv) inconvenience, discomfort, disappointment, hardship, frustration and mental stress in life."
21. Further, in Raj Kumar v. Ajay Kumar & another (2011) 1 SCC 343, Hon'ble Supreme Court of India laid down general principles for computation of compensation in injury cases.

entities.text: Raj Kumar v. Ajay Kumar & another (2011) 1 SCC 343
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
The relevant paras of the judgment are reproduced as under:
5 . T h e p r o v i s i o n s o f t h e M o t o r V e h i c l e s _____________________________________________________________ Act, 1988 ("the Act", for short)
makes it clear that the award must be just, which means that compensation should, to the extent possible, fully and adequately restore the claimant to the position prior to the accident.
The object of awarding damages is to make good the loss suffered as a result of wrong done as far as money can do so, in a fair, reasonable and equitable manner.

The court or the Tribunal shall have to assess the damages objectively and exclude from consideration any speculation or fancy, though some conjecture with reference to the nature of disability and its consequences, is inevitable.
A person is not only to be compensated for the physical injury, but also for the loss which he suffered as a result of such injury.

This means that he is to be compensated for his inability to lead a full life, his inability to enjoy those normal amenities which he would have enjoyed but for the injuries, and his inability to earn as much as he used to earn or could have earned.

6. The heads under which compensation is awarded in personal injury cases are the following:
Pecuniary Damages (special damages)

(i) Expenses relating to treatment, hospitalization, medicines, transportation,
nourishing food and miscellaneous expenditure.

(ii) Loss of earnings (and other gains) which the injured would have made had he not been injured, comprising:
(a) Loss of earning during the period of treatment.
(b) Loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability.
Preeti Rana (Injured) vs Rakesh (Driver) on 20 April, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/37672764/
7 (iii) Future medical expenses.
 Non-Pecuniary Damages (general  damages)
_____________________________________________________________ (iv) Damages to pain, suffering and trauma as a consequence of the injuries.
 (v) Loss of amenities (and/or loss of  prospects of marriage)
(vi) Loss of expectation of life (shortening of normal longevity).
In routine personal injury cases, compensation will be awarded only under heads (i),
(ii), (a) and (iv).

It is only in serious cases of injury, where there is specific medical evidence corroborating the evidence of the claimant, that compensation will be granted under any of the heads (ii), (b), (iii),
(v) and (vi) relating to loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability,
future medical expenses, loss of amenities (and/or loss of prospects of marriage) and loss of expectation of life.
22.

Therefore, a total sum of these bills, amounting to Rs.5,41,637/- is awarded to the petitioner under this head.

Loss of earning during treatment :
24.

Though petitioner, being a government employee, did not suffer any direct loss of income during her treatment but she claims reimbursement of 300 medical leaves which exhausted during her treatment on account of this accident.
As per evidence led by PW1 (petitioner) and PW5 (Head Master), petitioner was a permanent employee as Assistant Teacher in Primary School, Village Hisavada, Baghpat.
PW1 (petitioner) placed on record approval order, dated 17.02.2017, issued by her office.

Perusal of said order shows that District Basic Education Officer, Baghpat, had approved her medical leaves of 300 days (i.e. 91 days for the period from 06.01.2016 t o 0 5 . 0 4 . 2 0 1 6 ; 4 2 d a y s f o r t h e p e r i o d f r o m 0 7 . 0 4 . 2 0 1 6 t o _____________________________________________________________ 18.05.2016 and 167 days for the period from 08.07.2016 to 21.12.2016).
25.

It cannot be disputed that there had been no direct loss of income to the petitioner on account of aforesaid medical leaves but it cannot be ignored that said leaves deducted from her account could have been utilized by her in future in case of any need.

Consequently, after exhausting all her leaves or such a long period of leave on account of accident, she would be left with no or few unpaid leaves and in such circumstances, if she would need further leaves in future for medical/ unavoidable reasons, she would be compelled to go on unpaid leaves.

In case of Ramveer Singh vs.
Rajesh Kumar & Ors., MAC.APP. 12/2011, decided on 30.11.2012, Hon'ble High Court of Delhi held as under :
"6. ... A victim of a motor vehicle accident cannot be made to suffer loss of his full pay leave or the medical leave for the benefit of the tortfeasor.

Loss of Future Earnings due to disability:
27.

In case of Raj Kumar v. Ajay Kumar & Anr. (2011) 1 SCC 343, Hon'ble Supreme Court of India laid down broad criteria for assessment of permanent disability for ascertaining the purpose of future loss of earning was discussed and Hon'ble Apex Court laid down the principles for assessment of disability and for ascertainment to the effect of the permanent disability on the actual earning capacity, as under:-
13.

sentences.text:
We may now summarize the principles discussed above:
(i). All injuries (or permanent disabilities arising from injuries), do not result in loss of earning capacity.
( ii).
The percentage of permanent disability with reference to the whole body of a person, cannot be assumed to be the percentage of loss of earning capacity.

To put it differently, the percentage of loss of earning capacity is not the same as the percentage of permanent disability (except in a few cases, where the Tribunal on the basis of evidence, concludes that percentage of loss of earning capacity is the same as p e r c e n t a g e  
o f  
p e r m a n e n t _____________________________________________________________ disability).
(iii).
The doctor who treated an injured- claimant or who examined him subsequently to assess the extent of his permanent disability can give evidence only in regard the extent of permanent disability.
The loss of earning capacity is something that will have to be assessed by the Tribunal with reference to the evidence in entirety.

(iv). The same permanent disability may result in different percentages of loss of earning capacity in different persons, depending upon the nature of profession, occupation or job, age, education and other factors.

Dr. Shivam Saurav, Senior Resident, Orthopedic, GTB Hospital, Delhi, produced the record pertaining to disability certificate issued to petitioner vide no. 523/46/10/2021, dated 18.10.2021 Preeti Rana (Injured) vs Rakesh (Driver) on 20 April, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/37672764/
10 and proved the same as Ex.PW6/A, which makes it clear that petitioner has suffered 28% physical disability in relation to both lower limbs.

It is evident that petitioner is a government employee,
serving as a teacher in government school.

Therefore, taking into consideration that she has suffered 28% permanent physical disability in relation to both lower limb, now it is required to be seen that upto what extent the affected limbs would impact her earnings as a government teacher so that a just and reasonable compensation may be granted to him under this head.

It has been laid down in Raj Kumar (Supra), that:
"10.
......If the claimant was a driver or a carpenter, the actual loss of earning capacity may virtually be hundred percent, if he is neither able to drive or do carpentry.

On the other hand, if the claimant was a clerk in government service, the loss of his hand m a y n o t r e s u l t i n l o s s o f e m p l o y m e n t a n d h e m a y _____________________________________________________________ still be continued as a clerk as he could perform his clerical functions; and in that event the loss of earning capacity will not be 100% as in the case of a driver or carpenter, nor 60% which is the actual physical diability, but far less.

In fact, there may not be any need to award any compensation under the head of 'loss of future earnings', if the claimant continues in government service, though he may be awarded compensation under the head of loss of amenities as a consequence of loosing his hand.

Sometimes the injured claimant may be continued in service but may not found suitable for discharging the duties attached to the post or job which he was earlier holding, on account of his disability, and may therefore, be shifted to some other suitable but lesser post with lesser emoluments, in which case, there should be a limited award under the head of loss of future earning capacity taking note of the reduced earning capacity.

29. In view of the above proposition of law laid down by the Apex Court, it has to be kept in mind while determining the whole body functional disability for the purpose of awarding loss of future income, that the disablement and loss of earning capacity are two different aspects and not substitute to each other and the loss of income has to be seen considering the profession in which petitioner was engaged at the time of accident.
In this case, there is no evidence on record that petitioner had to/ will have to suffer any professional loss on account of injuries/ disability suffered in the accident.

No evidence has come on record that injuries/ disability would affect her chances of promotion or that she has been held to be not suitable for discharging her duties attached to the post of teacher on account of her disability.

Even after her r e t i r e m e n t  
f r o m  
t h e

Section 168 of Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 enjoins upon the claim Tribunal to hold an inquiry into the claim to make an award determining the amount of compensation, which appears to be just and reasonable.
As per settled law, compensation is not expected to be windfall or a bonanza nor it should be pittance
A man is not compensated for the physical injury, he is compensated for the loss which he suffers as a result of that injury (Baker v.
Willoughby (1970) Ac 467 at page 492 per Lord Reid).
21. Further, in Raj Kumar v. Ajay Kumar & another (2011) 1 SCC 343, Hon'ble Supreme Court of India laid down general principles for computation of compensation in injury cases.
makes it clear that the award must be just, which means that compensation should, to the extent possible, fully and adequately restore the claimant to the position prior to the accident.
The object of awarding damages is to make good the loss suffered as a result of wrong done as far as money can do so, in a fair, reasonable and equitable manner.
A person is not only to be compensated for the physical injury, but also for the loss which he suffered as a result of such injury.
This means that he is to be compensated for his inability to lead a full life, his inability to enjoy those normal amenities which he would have enjoyed but for the injuries, and his inability to earn as much as he used to earn or could have earned.
It cannot be disputed that there had been no direct loss of income to the petitioner on account of aforesaid medical leaves but it cannot be ignored that said leaves deducted from her account could have been utilized by her in future in case of any need.
In case of Ramveer Singh vs.
Rajesh Kumar & Ors., MAC.APP. 12/2011, decided on 30.11.2012, Hon'ble High Court of Delhi held as under :
"6. ... A victim of a motor vehicle accident cannot be made to suffer loss of his full pay leave or the medical leave for the benefit of the tortfeasor.
In view of above, this Tribunal is of the view that petitioner should be compensated for the aforesaid 300 medical leaves deducted by her office on account of the accident.
The percentage of permanent disability with reference to the whole body of a person, cannot be assumed to be the percentage of loss of earning capacity.
The doctor who treated an injured- claimant or who examined him subsequently to assess the extent of his permanent disability can give evidence only in regard the extent of permanent disability.
The loss of earning capacity is something that will have to be assessed by the Tribunal with reference to the evidence in entirety.
It is evident that petitioner is a government employee,
serving as a teacher in government school.
Therefore, taking into consideration that she has suffered 28% permanent physical disability in relation to both lower limb, now it is required to be seen that upto what extent the affected limbs would impact her earnings as a government teacher so that a just and reasonable compensation may be granted to him under this head.
29. In view of the above proposition of law laid down by the Apex Court, it has to be kept in mind while determining the whole body functional disability for the purpose of awarding loss of future income, that the disablement and loss of earning capacity are two different aspects and not substitute to each other and the loss of income has to be seen considering the profession in which petitioner was engaged at the time of accident.
In this case, there is no evidence on record that petitioner had to/ will have to suffer any professional loss on account of injuries/ disability suffered in the accident.
No evidence has come on record that injuries/ disability would affect her chances of promotion or that she has been held to be not suitable for discharging her duties attached to the post of teacher on account of her disability.
Thus, in the present case, I find no functional disability in relation to whole body of the petitioner for the purpose of determining the future loss of income to petitioner because she is not going to suffer any loss of future income due to the disability sustained by her in the accident.
